🌊🇺🇸 Trump’s Hormuz Pageant

Donald Trump posted the same image again: the Strait of Hormuz circled on a map and labeled “NEW U.S. TERRITORY.” No treaty. No annexation. Just a presidential marker pen having a maritime episode on Truth Social. It was the second time in a week he had shared it. 

Iran replied with a toy-block animation. This is the current contest over one of the world’s most consequential shipping chokepoints: a presidential graphic versus an animation.

Neither side should be taken at its word. Tehran calls the strait closed. Trump calls it American. The waterway remains legally international, and neither slogan answers the questions that matter: who can move cargo, how safely, and for how long. 

Beneath the performance, some ships are moving.

The New York Post, citing UK Maritime Trade Operations data, reported that nearly 200 vessels crossed Hormuz last week, up from about 150 the week before and roughly 40 two weeks earlier. That is an increase of almost 400 percent from the low point — but still only about one-fifth of prewar traffic. 

Oil firms from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates have reportedly hired tankers that turn off their transponders while using a U.S.-backed route near Oman. In other words, the Gulf’s oil is moving under American protection, provided it does not advertise its itinerary. 

That gives Trump material for the show: more hulls in the strait, a corridor that functions, a map ready for the cameras. It does not make Hormuz American territory, and it does not turn a volatile, partially reopened passage into a dependable victory.

But Iran supplied the day’s accounting problem. Its central bank said the Oil Ministry had deposited $7.5 billion in oil-sale and foreign-exchange proceeds over the first four months of the Iranian year. It does make the word “blockade” less straightforward. 

A blockade that still leaves billions reaching the central bank is not a slogan-proof reality. It is a contested system with leaks, exemptions, and very good accountants.

📣 EU to revise MiCA rules in 2027 amid US stablecoin push 

⚠️ European Union officials are preparing to revise the bloc’s MiCA crypto framework in 2027 as foreign stablecoin restrictions and faster U.S. rulemaking expose gaps in the existing regime. The planned revision would examine how MiCA treats stablecoins issued outside the European Union. Current requirements have prevented several foreign issuers from receiving authorization, limiting their access to regulated exchanges across the bloc.

💬 “Reopening the file seems unavoidable at this stage,” an unidentified European diplomat told Euronews.

🔗 The diplomat cited positions taken by European institutions, including the European Central Bank, along with changes in global regulation and digital-asset technology. No final proposal has been published. Any amendment would need to pass through the EU’s legislative process before taking effect. The consultation covers developments that have occurred since MiCA entered into application. Its deadline has been extended to Sept. 30, with crypto issuers, service providers, regulators, central banks and finance ministries invited to respond.

🇵🇸 “Palestine Exists,” Says Ra’am. The Denial Choir Begins.

Ra’am convened in Tayibe to select its Knesset slate and authorize party leader Mansour Abbas to reserve slots for possible recruits. Abbas opened with a statement designed to trip every Israeli coalition wire:

“The State of Palestine exists, and most of the world recognizes it, except for the United States and Israel. We want them to recognize it as well, and we are working to achieve peace, reconciliation and an end to the occupation and the conflict.” 

The conference approved a list led by Abbas, followed by Walid Taha, Walid al-Hawashla, Iman Khatib-Yassin, and Yasser Hujeirat. It also authorized Abbas to reserve places on the ticket while talks continue over a possible move by former Yesh Atid MK Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas said Segalovitz would be suited to serve as national security minister; Segalovitz has not formally joined Ra’am. 

Then Israel’s political class began racing each other to reject the premise.

Gadi Eisenkot wrote: “There is no Palestinian state, and under a government we establish, no Palestinian state will be created.” 

Benjamin Netanyahu seized on the same line. “As long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state controlled by Iran: not in Gaza, and not in Judea and Samaria. Period.” He then cast Abbas as proof of the danger posed by a prospective left-wing coalition with the Muslim Brotherhood. 

The point is not that Abbas, Eisenkot, and Netanyahu agree on Palestinian statehood. They plainly do not. Abbas’s line became raw political material: Ra’am offered recognition; Eisenkot offered refusal; Netanyahu turned both into a campaign argument about coalition arithmetic.

The Joint List is watching from the Arab flank. Its chairman, Yousef Jabareen, says the reunited alliance expects more than 10 seats in the next election and claims Ra’am was invited to join but “was not serious.” Ra’am, meanwhile, is betting that Abbas’s route still runs through a future governing coalition. 

In Israeli election politics, a Palestinian state can be a legal fact, a security threat, an impossible promise, and a coalition weapon — often inside a single news cycle.
